newsitem.title: GERMANY: Spiegel says Tietmeyer asks whether can delay EMU.
newsitem.headline: Spiegel says Tietmeyer asks whether can delay EMU.

text.p: Germany's Der Spiegel magazine said on Saturday that Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer has asked whether Germany and France can consider delaying the start of European monetary union (EMU) set for January 1, 1999.

Spiegel, citing unnamed sources, said in an article released ahead of publication that Tietmeyer did not believe it would be wrong if currency union were delayed if entry criteria were not met in time by Bonn and Paris for the 1999 start.
"Wouldn't it be a possibility, together with France, to agree to a delay in the start of the euro," the magazine quoted Tietmeyer as saying in an article to be published this week.

Spiegel, citing unnamed sources, said in the article released ahead of publication that Tietmeyer did not believe it would be wrong if currency union were delayed if Bonn and Paris did not meet entry criteria this year for the 1999 start.
A Bundesbank spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment on the Spiegel article.

But German central bank sources have said the question of delaying currency union should not be made into a total taboo if either Germany or France, considered to be key members, failed to meet entry criteria in the Maastricht Treaty.
Tietmeyer has also not made the case in the past for a delay in currency union but has simply asked the question as to whether this should be considered, bank sources have said.
A Spiegel spokesman said the magazine had not spoken directly with Tietmeyer, saying the information was based on sources in Germany. He declined further comment.

Prospects for an EMU delay rose last week after Bonn and the Bundesbank openly clashed over Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plans to revalue the bank's reserves and demand a payout of the hidden profits to help Bonn meet the criteria.
The Bundesbank, a fierce proponent of fiscal austerity in meeting the criteria for monetary union, on Wednesday opening critcised Waigel's plan and said it could undermine the euro from the start.
